1. Introduction                                                                       Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts

Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
have established them as powerful foundation models                 Figure 2. Our model, G2 VLM, employs an architecture inspired
across a wide range of tasks [6, 43, 64, 82]. Yet several           by the two-streams hypothesis. It features two experts: a geomet-
studies [10, 20, 52, 79] have found that VLMs exhibit a sig-        ric perception expert (our “where pathway”) for visual geometry
                                                                    learning and a semantic perception expert (our “what pathway”)
nificant gap in robust spatial understanding, a crucial capa-
                                                                    for multimodal understanding.
bility for spatial intelligence, robotics, and embodied AI.
    We argue that this limitation stems from how current

VLMs acquire their physical world knowledge. Their spa-

tial understanding is largely gained implicitly from training

primarily on language and 2D visual priors. Except incor-

general VLMs simply employ feature projection layers                    To train both experts effectively, G2 VLM employs a

tions into a coherent 3D representation of the world, which         dataset to learn a geometry-rich representation. In the sec-

2. Related Works                                                        the limitations of 2D data priors, other recent works have
VLMs as Unified Foundation Models Recent advance-                       noted the lack of geometric features in VLMs. For exam-
ments in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have trans-                      ple, VLM-3R [21] and Spatial MLLM [69] both integrate
formed multimodal research into a foundation-model                      a frozen geometry encoder (e.g., VGGT) as an extra repre-
paradigm. By combining visual understanding and lan-                    sentation and train the VLM to learn from these features.
guage generation, VLMs demonstrates zero-shot general-                  In contrast, our work directly integrates a geometric expert
izability across a wide range of multimodal tasks [23, 24,              within our VLM, which offers a more natural alignment and
32, 83]. More recently, VLMs are being further unified                  unifies visual geometry prediction tasks with high-level spa-
to handle diverse tasks in an Any-to-Any input and output               tial reasoning. Our model natively supports both geometric
paradigm spanning audio, image, and video [33, 41, 71, 76].             and semantic perception and can serve as a strong baseline

ing and interleaved reasoning. This is achieved by optimiz-           metric perception expert, we further divide it into two stage

explore three distinct joint-training strategies, where the se-       (lr) of 2e-4 using cosine scheduler. Then we further train at
mantic perception expert is, by default, optimized using a            lr of 5e-4 for another 20K steps with a higher resolution
cross-entropy (CE) loss:                                              of 518x518, and apply randomized aspect ratio between

  only the semantic perception expert is updated. This                domly sample 2–24 frames from a random training scene.

  the visual geometry performance unaltered.                          3 days. For joint-training, we use AdamW optimizer for

  with CE loss. This fine-tunes the geometry features ex-             days. Throughout all training, we employ gradient norm

Camera Pose Estimation. Following prior work [57, 62],
                                                                    4.3. Discussions and Ablation Study
we evaluate predicted camera poses on the Co3Dv2 [46]
dataset, which features over 1000 test sequences, using an-         In our work, we adopt a dual-expert design comprising two
gular accuracy. For each sequence, we randomly sample               distinct experts: one for geometric perception and one for
10 images, form all possible pairs, and compute the angular         semantic perception. This naturally raises several research

    In contrast to VGGT, which relies on a computationally
intensive DPT head that aggregates multi-scale features, we          C. More results
adopt lightweight transformer-based geometry heads which
is similar to π 3 . The decoders for camera poses, local point       We evaluate our model on the SPAR-Bench which is a com-
maps, and global point maps, share the same trasformer ar-           prehensive spatial reasoning benchmark. Here we present
chitecture but do not share weights. This architecture is a          the detailed results of each sub-task in SPAR-Bench in Ta-
lightweight, 5-layer transformer that applies self-attention         ble 3. Our model, G2 VLM-SR, demonstrates the best per-

heads for local point maps consist of a simple MLP fol-
lowed by a pixel shuffle operation. For camera poses, the
head is adapted from Reloc3r [19] and Pi3 [67] and uses
an MLP, average pooling, and another MLP. The rotation
is initially predicted in a 9D representation [30] and is then
converted to a 3×3 rotation matrix via SVD orthogonaliza-
tion. As we mentioned in Sec 3.1, the global point head
serves solely to stabilize training and is excluded during in-
ference.

B. Training Details
For the pre-training stage of geometric perception expert,
we further divide it into two stage training. We first fix im-
age resolution to 224x224 and use AdamW optimizer for
100K iterations with a learning rate (lr) of 2e-4 using cosine
scheduler. Then we further train at lr of 5e-4 for another
20K steps with a higher resolution of 518x518, and apply
randomized aspect ratio between 0.5 and 1.0. Similar to
VGGT, for every batch, we randomly sample 2–24 frames
from a random training scene. For our visual geometry loss
function, we set the weights for each component as follows:
λnormal = 1.0, λcam = 0.2, and λtrans = 200.0. The im-
plementation of our normal loss follows that of MoGe [61]
and π 3 [67], and the resolution for aligning the local point
map loss is set to 4096. The low-resolution pretraining runs

Table 3. Performance of different models on SPAR-Bench The highest, second-highest, and third-highest scores in each category are
highlighted with light red , light orange , and light yellow , respectively. SPAR-Bench (tiny) refers to a subset of the full benchmark,
where 50 questions are sampled per task. Our model, G2 VLM-SR, demonstrate the best performance consistently across all tasks. Notably,
it surpasses human performance in low category.
